The nested estimate measures how well a whole tuning procedure (tune,
select, fit) performs on new data. The worked example is in
`vignette("nested-cv")`.

## Why the tuned score is optimistic

When we tune with cross-validation, we score several candidates (the
settings tried) and keep the best. Scores are noisy, so the best of
several tends to look better than it is. The winner's score overstates how
the model will do on new data.

Nested resampling moves the tuning inside each outer fold. Each fold
tunes, selects and fits on its own analysis rows, then scores the chosen
setting once on assessment rows that the tuning never saw.

## What the estimate describes

The mean from `collect_metrics()` is the error of the procedure when it
trains on each fold's analysis rows and predicts new data.

The estimate describes the procedure, not one fitted model, and we report
it for the deployed model because `nested_final_fit()` runs that procedure
on all the data. No rows remain that the final fit did not see, so there
is no second number to compute.

The estimate is not a score of the parameter values the final fit chose.
It is also the error on this data set, not the average over every training
set the same source can produce. Luo and Barber (2026) prove that any
assumption-free test of that average needs far more data than the
training set holds, so this package offers no such test.

## Where a test set fits

A test set gives one number from one split. The outer folds give a mean
and show how much the score moves between folds. We can keep both.

We split with `initial_split()` and run the nested loop and
`nested_final_fit()` on `training()`. Then we score the final model's
predictions on `testing()` once, as `last_fit()` does after ordinary
tuning. We report the test score for that fitted model, and the nested
estimate for the procedure that made it.

## Choosing the number of folds

Arlot and Celisse (2010) report that 5 to 10 folds is the usual advice
for model selection, which is the inner loop's job. They add that the best
count depends on the problem.

More outer folds give each model more training rows, and each outer fold
adds a whole tuning run. `vignette("nested-cv")` counts the fits.

## A slight pessimism

Each outer model trains on fewer rows than the deployed model, so the
estimate tends to look a little worse than the procedure deserves. Varma
and Simon (2006) ran nested cross-validation on 40 samples with no signal,
where the true error was 50.0%. The nested estimate was 54.2%, and they
attribute the gap to training on 39 rows rather than 40.

On 41,121 hospital visits, Wilimitis and Walsh (2023) found nested
cross-validation among the most pessimistic methods, by 1 to 2% of AUROC
and 5 to 9% of AUPR. The gap is a property of the method, so it
is no reason to adjust the reported number.

## The standard error

`std_err` is the standard error of the mean across the outer folds. It
measures the precision of the mean, not the spread of the folds. It treats
the fold scores as independent, but the folds share training rows, so it
tends to understate the uncertainty. Bengio and Grandvalet (2004) prove
that no estimator of this variance is unbiased in every case, so the
package builds no interval from it.

## Comparing workflows

A gap between two nested estimates is a reason to look closer, never a
result. Bayle et al. (2026) show that two stable procedures can have an
unstable difference. Picking the best of a set from `nested_workflow_map()` is itself a
selection that no outer loop scored, so the package ranks none.

## When the folds disagree

When the folds choose different values for a parameter, the data does not
pin that value down. The estimate still holds, because it averages over
that variation. For two similar candidates, the comparison itself is
unstable (Bayle et al., 2026), so which one wins a fold says little.

## When nesting pays

Nesting matters most when the search had room to overfit. Tibshirani and
Tibshirani (2009) tuned on pure noise, where the true error is 50%. With
400 rows and 100 features, the tuned score was under 3 points too good.

With 40 rows and 1000 features, nearest shrunken centroids read 38.4%,
11.6 points too good, while an SVM was 2.5 points too good and a tree 0.2.
That paper's remedy is a correction, not nesting.

Nesting adds little with many rows and a small grid. Wilimitis and Walsh
(2023) found no gain there, only extra cost. More rows alone do not
remove the bias. Vabalas et al. (2019) saw
cross-validation without nesting beat chance on pure noise at 1000 rows.

Feature selection belongs in the recipe, so the loop repeats it in every
fold. A step run on the data before the call is not repeated, and no
result can show it. Vabalas et al. (2019) found that selection outside the
loop does more harm than tuning outside it.

for model selection. *Statistics Surveys*, 4, 40–79.

Bayle, A., Janson, L., & Mackey, L. (2026). The relative instability of
model comparison with cross-validation. *arXiv:2508.04409*.

1089–1105.

learning algorithm validation with a limited sample size. *PLoS ONE*,
